title: Pay Per Call Software: 7 Features to Look For
h1: Pay per call software: what to look for before you choose
description: Choosing pay per call software? Use this 7-point checklist on tracking, routing, bidding, quality and payouts to pick a platform that fits your network.
faq: What features should pay per call software have?

At minimum: call tracking with dynamic number insertion, routing rules for buyer hours, caps and states, quality controls for short or repeat calls, per-affiliate payouts with statements, and integrations such as webhooks and an API. Real-time bidding matters if your calls vary in value.
How much does pay per call software cost?

It depends on the platform and your volume. Insight Dial is pay as you go: a per-minute call rate plus a monthly price per tracking number, paid from a topped-up balance. Quotes are available on request at insightdial.com/pricing.
Do I need real-time bidding or is a waterfall enough?

A waterfall works well for fixed agreements with a set order of buyers. Real-time bidding helps when some callers are worth much more than others and several buyers want them. Many publishers use both on different campaigns.
body:
Good pay per call software does five jobs well: it tracks every call back to the source that sent it, routes each call to the right buyer in real time, filters out low-quality and repeat calls before they cost anyone money, pays affiliates accurately, and gives buyers and partners a record they trust. If a platform is weak at any one of these, you will feel it in disputes, missed revenue or hours of spreadsheet work. Use the checklist below to judge any option before you commit live traffic to it.

What to look for in pay per call software

Start with the problems you actually have. A publisher sending calls to a handful of fixed buyers needs strong routing and caps. A network managing dozens of affiliates needs payouts and portals. A team selling calls whose value changes caller to caller needs bidding. Most growing operations end up needing all three, so it pays to choose software that covers the full chain from the first ring to the final statement. If you are new to the model, our guide to what pay per call is explains who sits on each side of a call.

1. Accurate call tracking and attribution

Every payout and every buyer invoice depends on knowing where a call came from. Look for tracking numbers per source or campaign and dynamic number insertion, which swaps the number shown on a web page so each visitor's call can be tied back to the traffic that brought them. Without it, you are guessing which ads and affiliates are working.

2. Routing rules that match your buyer agreements

Buyers rarely take calls around the clock from everywhere. Your software should let you set a routing order (a waterfall) and enforce each buyer's terms automatically:

  • Hours so calls only reach buyers when they are open
  • Daily caps so a buyer never receives more calls than they agreed to
  • State rules for buyers licensed or interested in specific states
  • Blocked numbers and repeat-caller blocks so the same person is not sold twice
  • A pre-transfer check that confirms a buyer can take the call before it is sent

When these rules live in the platform instead of in someone's head, fewer calls are rejected and fewer invoices are disputed.

3. Real-time bidding for calls with variable value

A fixed price for every call leaves money on the table when some callers are worth far more than others. With real-time bidding, several buyers are asked for a price at the same moment and the highest bid above your minimum wins. Check two details: how fast the auction finishes while the caller waits, and what happens when nobody bids. A good system falls back to your next option rather than dropping the call. Our explainer on how real-time call bidding works walks through the mechanics.

4. Quality controls that protect buyer relationships

Buyers leave when they receive too many short or junk calls. Look for a clear quality grade on each traffic source and the ability to pause a source automatically when it starts sending too many short calls. Call transcription with short summaries also helps: instead of listening to hours of recordings, you can scan what each call was about and settle questions quickly.

5. Payouts, portals and statements

If you work with affiliates, payout errors are the fastest way to lose them. Your software should support a different payout rate per affiliate, give affiliates and buyers their own portal to see their calls, and produce downloadable statements. When everyone reads from the same record, month-end becomes a check rather than an argument.

6. Integrations, alerts and security

Calls rarely live in one system. Signed webhooks with a delivery log let you push call events into your CRM or reporting tools and confirm they arrived, and an open API lets developers build on top. Alerts in the chat tools your team already uses mean you hear about a paused source or a capped buyer in minutes, not days. Two-step sign-in should be standard for any account that controls money and traffic.

7. Clear, usage-based pricing

Ask exactly what you pay for. Pay-as-you-go pricing, where you pay a per-minute call rate and a monthly price per tracking number, keeps costs tied to the traffic you actually run. Make sure you can get a quote for your expected volume before you start.

Questions to ask before you switch

  • Can I set every buyer's hours, caps and state rules without a support ticket?
  • What happens to a call when no buyer is available or nobody bids?
  • How will I spot a bad traffic source before a buyer complains?
  • Can affiliates and buyers see their own calls and statements?
  • Can I test a full call path before going live?

If a platform answers all five clearly, it is worth a closer look.
